title: WHAT IF EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT HELL IS WRONG? THE TERRIFYING QUESTION JESUS REFUSED TO LET US IGNORE
paragraphs: WHAT IF EVERYTHING YOU BELIEVE ABOUT HELL IS WRONG? THE TERRIFYING QUESTION JESUS REFUSED TO LET US IGNORE

Eternal torment? Final destruction? Or something far more complicated than we've been told? A journey into the original words of Scripture, the justice of God, the reality of judgment, and the astonishing grace of Jesus Christ.
There is a question most Christians are afraid to ask out loud.
Not because they don't believe the Bible.
But because they do.
And somewhere between the sermons they've heard, the funerals they've attended, and the people they love who still don't know Jesus, a question has been quietly haunting them.
What actually happens to someone who dies without Christ?
Do they remain conscious forever, experiencing punishment that never ends?
Does God finally destroy them so completely that they cease to exist?
Or have we misunderstood something about judgment, eternity, and the words Jesus Himself spoke?
Imagine standing beside the hospital bed of someone you love.
Their breathing is getting weaker.
You have prayed for them. You have spoken to them about Jesus. You have begged God to open their heart.
But you don't know what happened between their soul and God.
And then the monitor goes silent.
Suddenly, hell isn't a theological argument anymore.
It has a face.
A name.
A voice you will never hear again in this life.
And the question that once belonged to scholars now sits like a stone inside your chest.
God, what happens now?
Before we go any further, understand something.
We are not going to soften the warnings of Jesus to make Christianity more comfortable.
But neither are we going to make God appear more cruel than Scripture actually reveals.
We will not pretend that every difficult passage has an easy answer.
And we will not build our theology on frightening pictures, religious traditions, or emotional preferences when the written Word of God deserves to speak for itself.
Because the question isn't what version of hell makes us feel better.
The question is what God has actually revealed.
And the answer requires us to walk through some of the most sobering words ever spoken by Jesus Christ.
In Matthew 25:46, Jesus says:
“And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.” (KJV)
The Greek text reads:
Καὶ ἀπελεύσονται οὗτοι εἰς κόλασιν αἰώνιον, οἱ δὲ δίκαιοι εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον.
Kai apeleusontai houtoi eis kolasin aiōnion, hoi de dikaioi eis zōēn aiōnion.
The two expressions that demand our attention are κόλασιν αἰώνιον (kolasin aiōnion) and ζωὴν αἰώνιον (zōēn aiōnion).
Eternal punishment.
Eternal life.
The same adjective, aiōnion, describes both destinies.
And that matters.

The Greek adjective aiōnios is related to aiōn, a word associated with an age or an extended period of time. Depending on its context, aiōnios can express what belongs to an age or what is everlasting.
But here is where we must be careful.
It is not linguistically sound to insist that aiōnios can never mean everlasting.
Nor is it sound to assume that the word alone settles every question about the nature of punishment.
In Matthew 25:46, the parallel between eternal punishment and eternal life strongly supports the permanence of both outcomes.
But permanence of punishment and the precise experience of those punished are not identical questions.
And this is where sincere, Bible-believing Christians have disagreed.
Some understand eternal punishment as an everlasting, conscious experience of judgment.
Others understand it as a punishment whose irreversible result is eternal—the final loss of life.
Both interpretations must answer to the whole counsel of Scripture.
Neither should be dismissed through slogans.
And neither should be accepted merely because it is the position we inherited.
Think about that for a moment.
If Jesus warned us about something this serious, shouldn't we care enough to examine what He actually said?
The first major interpretation is called eternal conscious punishment.
This has been a prominent teaching throughout much of historic Christianity and is explicitly affirmed in several major Christian confessional traditions.
According to this understanding, those finally condemned remain conscious under God's righteous judgment without end.
Its defenders point first to the direct parallel in Matthew 25:46.
If the life of the righteous continues forever, they argue, the punishment of the wicked likewise continues forever.
They also point to Mark 9:47–48, where Jesus warns about Gehenna, speaking of the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched.
Those images draw from Isaiah 66:24, where the prophet describes the corpses of those who rebelled against God.
That Old Testament background is important.
Isaiah's immediate picture is of dead bodies exposed to shame and destruction, not an explicit description of immortal souls suffering.
Yet Jesus uses this dreadful imagery to communicate the seriousness of final judgment.
Those who defend eternal conscious punishment understand the unending worm and unquenchable fire as pointing beyond physical destruction to a judgment that does not cease.
Those who defend final destruction understand the same imagery as emphasizing a judgment that cannot be stopped until its work is complete.
The disagreement is not whether Jesus warned about judgment.
He absolutely did.
The disagreement is what the imagery teaches about the final condition of the condemned.
Then comes Revelation.
And the language becomes even more frightening.
Revelation 14:11 says:
“And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night...” (KJV)
Revelation 20:10 describes the devil, the beast, and the false prophet being tormented day and night forever and ever.
These are among the strongest biblical passages used to defend eternal conscious punishment.
We should not minimize them.
But we must also notice the precise subjects and contexts of these statements.
Revelation 20:10 explicitly names the devil, the beast, and the false prophet.
Revelation 14:9–11 describes those who worship the beast and receive its mark, and its language is central to the debate over human judgment.
Interpreters disagree about how literally the apocalyptic imagery should be understood and how these passages relate to the final judgment of all the wicked.
Revelation is not a book we should read carelessly.
Its visions are filled with symbolic beasts, heavenly scenes, prophetic imagery, and Old Testament allusions.
Symbolism does not make judgment unreal.
But it does mean that we must interpret the images responsibly.
For example, the language of rising smoke recalls Isaiah 34:9–10, where Edom's judgment is portrayed with smoke ascending perpetually.
The imagery communicates devastating, irreversible divine judgment.
Does Revelation use that language to describe an ongoing conscious experience, or to portray the everlasting testimony of an accomplished destruction?
Christians have argued both ways.
The debate cannot be settled merely by saying, “It's obviously symbolic,” or, “It's obviously literal.”
We must ask what the symbols mean.
And then we reach a verse that changes the direction of the conversation.
Revelation 20:14 says:
“And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος
ho thanatos ho deuteros.
The second death.
Not simply the second suffering.
Not explicitly the second kind of conscious existence.
The second death.
The full expression in Revelation 20:14 identifies the lake of fire with this second death.
Then Revelation 20:15 says that anyone not found written in the book of life is cast into the lake of fire.
The implications are staggering.
Because Scripture does not merely call this final destiny punishment.
It calls it death.
But what does death mean here?
Does it mean the final destruction of the person?
Or does it mean an everlasting condition of separation and judgment, described as death because it is the ultimate loss of blessed life with God?
This is one of the central questions.
Those who defend conditional immortality, often associated with annihilationism, argue that human beings are not inherently indestructible and that immortality is ultimately God's gift.
They point to Romans 6:23:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” (KJV)
Notice the contrast.
Death.
Eternal life.
Not explicitly eternal life in misery versus eternal life in happiness.
Death versus life.
They also point to Matthew 10:28, where Jesus warns:
“...fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.” (KJV)
The Greek verb translated “destroy” is ἀπολέσαι (apolesai), from apollymi.
The word can refer to destruction, ruin, loss, or perishing, depending on context.
It does not always mean annihilation.
For example, the same verb family can describe something lost that is later found.
But Matthew 10:28 is still significant because Jesus speaks of God being able to destroy both body and soul in Gehenna.
Conditionalists argue that this language fits final destruction more naturally than everlasting preservation in torment.
Defenders of eternal conscious punishment respond that destruction can refer to ruin or the loss of well-being without requiring cessation of existence.
Both sides must explain the wording rather than merely assuming their conclusion.
Then consider John 3:16, perhaps the most beloved verse in the Bible.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” (KJV)
The Greek verb behind “perish” is ἀπόληται (apolētai), also from apollymi.
Once again, we encounter the contrast between perishing and everlasting life.
The verse certainly teaches that salvation is found through faith in God's Son.
But it does not, by itself, settle every philosophical question about the final state of the lost.
What it does make unmistakably clear is this:
Eternal life is not something sinners can demand. It is a gift received through Jesus Christ.
And no matter which interpretation of final punishment one finds most persuasive, the loss described in these passages is unimaginably serious.
Now listen to the prophet Malachi.
Malachi 4:1 describes the coming day of judgment as a burning oven, when the arrogant and evildoers will be like stubble.
The Hebrew includes the expression:
kaqqash.
“Like stubble.”
Something dry.
Fragile.
Ready to burn.
Malachi says the coming day will leave them neither root nor branch.
Then Malachi 4:3 portrays the wicked as ashes beneath the feet of the righteous.
Those who believe in final destruction see these images as powerful evidence that the wicked ultimately perish rather than remain alive forever in torment.
Those who believe in eternal conscious punishment understand the images as prophetic pictures of total defeat and judgment, not necessarily literal descriptions of the extinction of persons.
Again, the disagreement concerns how the imagery relates to final reality.
And it is precisely here that Christians must resist a temptation.
The temptation to make our preferred interpretation sound as though no faithful reader of Scripture could possibly disagree.
Because humility is not compromise.
And careful interpretation is not unbelief.
But there is another position we must examine.
One that raises perhaps the most emotionally appealing possibility of all.
What if God's final judgment ultimately results in the restoration of every person?
This view is commonly called universal reconciliation or universal salvation, although its different advocates do not agree on every detail.
Some believe postmortem judgment is real and severe but ultimately corrective.
Others emphasize God's final victory over all rebellion.
Supporters frequently appeal to passages such as Colossians 1:20, where God is said to reconcile all things to Himself through Christ, making peace through the blood of His cross.
They also point to 1 Corinthians 15:22:
“For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” (KJV)
And Philippians 2:10–11, which declares that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.
These are magnificent declarations of Christ's cosmic supremacy.
But do they promise the eventual salvation of every individual?
That is disputed.
In 1 Corinthians 15, the surrounding discussion concerns resurrection, Christ's victory over death, and the ordering of those who belong to Him.
In Philippians 2, universal acknowledgment of Christ's lordship does not explicitly establish that every confession is a saving confession.

And in Colossians 1, interpreters disagree about whether the reconciliation of all things entails the salvation of every rebellious person or the restoration of cosmic order under Christ's victorious authority.
Those who reject universal salvation also point to passages describing final exclusion, destruction, and eternal punishment.
Matthew 25:46 remains a serious challenge.
So does Revelation 20:15.
And so does Jesus' warning in Matthew 7:13–14 about the broad way leading to destruction and the narrow way leading to life.
Christian universalism has appeared in some streams of Christian thought, but it has not been the dominant position of historic Christian orthodoxy.
It should not be presented as an established conclusion of Scripture.
Yet neither should we pretend that the passages its advocates raise are unworthy of serious study.
The Bible's declarations about God's saving purpose, Christ's victory, and the restoration of creation deserve careful attention.
But we cannot turn a hope, an inference, or an unresolved theological argument into a promise God has not clearly given.
And here is where this entire discussion becomes deeply personal.
Because behind every interpretation is a question about God's character.
Can God be perfectly just and perfectly loving?
Can He judge evil without becoming evil?
Can His mercy be genuine if His judgment is terrifying?
And can we trust Him with the people we cannot save?
Scripture's answer begins not with our preferred model of hell.
It begins with the character of the Judge.
Genesis 18:25 asks:
“Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
הֲשֹׁפֵט כָּל־הָאָרֶץ לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפָּט
Hashofet kol-ha'arets lo ya'aseh mishpat?
The question appeals to God's righteousness.
And the entire biblical witness affirms that God's judgments are just.
Deuteronomy 32:4 calls Him a God of truth, without iniquity, just and right.
Psalm 89:14 declares that righteousness and judgment are the foundation of His throne.
Ezekiel 33:11 records God's declaration that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but calls the wicked to turn and live.
And 2 Peter 3:9 describes the Lord as patient, not wishing that any should perish but that all should come to repentance.
These passages do not erase the warnings about final judgment.
They reveal the heart of the God who gives those warnings.
God is not a sadist delighting in human suffering.
He is not morally indifferent to cruelty, exploitation, betrayal, abuse, or rebellion.
And His love is not a sentimental refusal to confront evil.
Imagine a world in which every murderer, every trafficker, every abuser, and every destroyer of innocent lives could continue forever without judgment.
Would that be love?
Would that be justice?
Would the victims call that goodness?
The Bible says God will judge the world in righteousness.
But the same Bible reveals a God who calls sinners to repentance, receives the contrite, and sent His Son into the world to save.
This is not a contradiction in God's character.
It is the terrifying beauty of His holiness and mercy.
And nowhere do those realities meet more powerfully than at the cross.
Picture Calvary.
The sky darkening.
The crowd watching.
The religious leaders mocking.
The soldiers dividing garments.
And Jesus, bleeding beneath the weight of a Roman execution.
The One through whom all things were made is hanging between criminals.
He has touched lepers.
Forgiven sinners.
Welcomed the rejected.
Confronted hypocrites.
Wept over Jerusalem.
And now He is being crucified.
Not because He committed evil.
But because the sinless Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares that He was wounded for our transgressions and bruised for our iniquities.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
First Peter 3:18 says Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God.
Do not miss that.
Jesus did not come merely to provide information about judgment. He came to save sinners from judgment and reconcile them to God.
And this is where the theological argument must kneel before the Gospel.
Because whether the final punishment of the wicked involves unending conscious suffering or irreversible destruction, neither possibility should ever be treated casually.
Both are terrible.
Both communicate a loss beyond anything we should willingly risk.
And both should drive us toward the Savior rather than into pride over winning an argument.
There is something profoundly wrong when Christians can spend hours arguing about the duration of punishment while remaining indifferent to the people Jesus commanded us to love.
We can defend our interpretation.
Quote Greek.
Compare manuscripts.
Debate the meaning of aiōnios.
And still fail to obey the Lord who said to make disciples of all nations.
What good is being intellectually victorious if our hearts have grown cold?
What good is possessing a carefully developed doctrine of judgment if we no longer grieve over sin, pray for the lost, or proclaim the grace of Christ?
And what good is winning an online debate if we humiliate the very people we hope will hear the Gospel?
Jesus never treated eternal realities as entertainment.
He warned.
He wept.
He called people to repent.
And He gave His life.
Luke 19:41 tells us that when Jesus drew near Jerusalem, He wept over the city.
The Greek verb is ἔκλαυσεν (eklausen).
He wept.
The Lord who spoke about judgment also shed tears over those who would not recognize the things that made for their peace.
That should change the way we speak about hell.
Not with arrogance.
Not with delight.
Not with careless speculation about which particular people are condemned.
But with trembling conviction and genuine compassion.
Some of you reading this have spent years afraid that a loved one who died without an obvious confession of faith is beyond mercy.
You replay their final conversations.
You wonder whether they prayed silently.
Whether they remembered a Scripture.
Whether something happened in their heart during their final moments.
And the uncertainty hurts.
Scripture does not authorize us to declare someone saved simply because we loved them.
But neither does it authorize us to pronounce final condemnation on a particular person when God has not revealed that person's ultimate standing before Him.
God knows what we do not.
He sees the heart.
He judges justly.
And His knowledge is not limited by the moments we happened to witness.
We must not invent a second chance after death as though Scripture clearly promises one.
Hebrews 9:27 speaks of death followed by judgment.
But we also must not pretend that our limited knowledge gives us access to God's final verdict over every individual.
There is a difference between trusting God's mercy and claiming certainty where He has not given it.
Sometimes faith means placing unanswered questions into the hands of the One whose character has been revealed in Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the hardest prayer is simply:
Lord, You know what I do not. You are righteous where my understanding is incomplete. I entrust what I cannot see to You.
But if you are alive and reading this, there is another question that cannot wait.
Not what happened to someone else.
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
Because the Bible never tells us to postpone repentance until we have resolved every mystery of eternity.
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Mark 1:15 with a call to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek words are:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
Repent and believe in the Gospel.
The verb metanoeite calls for repentance—a genuine turning of mind and life toward God.
And pisteuete calls for faith, trust in the good news.
Not merely fear of punishment.
Not merely emotional panic.
Not merely repeating religious words to escape consequences.
But turning to the living Christ in faith.
You do not need to solve every theological disagreement before coming to Jesus.
You do not need to become morally perfect before asking for mercy.
You do not need to pretend your sins are smaller than they are.
You come because He is the Savior.
You repent because sin is real.
You believe because His death and resurrection are the foundation of Christian hope.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And Romans 10:9 speaks of confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead.
This is the Gospel.
Not that hell is imaginary.
Not that judgment is unimportant.
Not that everyone automatically receives eternal life regardless of their response to Christ.
But that God has acted in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners, forgive sins, defeat death, and bring those who trust Him into everlasting life.
Now return to our original question.
Does the Bible teach eternal conscious punishment, final destruction, or something else?

The most responsible answer is that Scripture unquestionably teaches final divine judgment, the seriousness of sin, the reality of exclusion from the life of God's kingdom, and the everlasting significance of our response to Christ.
The precise nature of the final punishment of the wicked remains a significant interpretive disagreement among Christians.
Eternal conscious punishment has substantial biblical arguments, particularly Matthew 25:46 and Revelation 14:9–11.

Conditional immortality and final destruction also have substantial biblical arguments, particularly Matthew 10:28, Romans 6:23, the destruction imagery of Malachi 4, and Revelation's description of the second death.
Universal reconciliation appeals to important biblical themes of cosmic restoration and divine victory, but faces serious difficulties in passages describing final judgment and permanent exclusion.
These positions are not interchangeable, and the weight of the arguments is debated.
We should study them seriously.
We should be willing to correct our understanding.
And we should refuse to manipulate Scripture to make it say what we want.
But there is a truth more important than our ability to settle every contested detail.
The Judge of the living and the dead is Jesus Christ.
Acts 17:31 declares that God has appointed a day to judge the world in righteousness through the Man He has ordained, giving assurance through His resurrection.
The One who judges is the One who bore the cross.
The One who warns is the One who invites.
The One who speaks of eternal life is the One who rose from the grave.
And that changes everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about choosing the least frightening theory of hell.
It is about knowing the risen Savior.
It is about sinners being reconciled to God.
It is about grace triumphing over the guilt we could never remove ourselves.
It is about a new heart.
A transformed life.
A forgiveness we did not earn.
And a hope that does not collapse at the grave.
Perhaps you opened this article expecting an argument.
Perhaps you wanted someone to prove your denomination right.
Perhaps you came looking for a verse that would finally silence someone who disagrees with you.
But what if God is using this moment to expose something deeper?
Perhaps you know the vocabulary of theology but have neglected prayer.
Perhaps you can explain the lake of fire but cannot remember the last time you spoke gently to someone who doubts.
Perhaps you have been so occupied with the fate of the lost that you have forgotten to love the lost.
Or perhaps you are the person who has been running from Christ.
You know the Scriptures.
You remember the sermons.
You remember the conviction you felt when you were younger.
But somewhere along the way, you learned to quiet the voice of conscience.
You told yourself there would always be more time.
One more year.
One more season.
One more opportunity to make things right.
Yet no one reading this has been promised tomorrow.
And the mercy of God should never become an excuse to delay repentance.
Second Corinthians 6:2 says:
“...behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” (KJV)
Now.
Not when your life becomes convenient.
Not when your questions are all answered.
Not when your past becomes less embarrassing.
Now.
If you are weary, come to Christ.
If you are ashamed, come to Christ.
If you have hidden your sins behind religious language, stop pretending and come to Christ.
If you have wandered far from the faith you once professed, hear His call to repent and return.
And if you are still searching, open the Gospels and encounter Jesus in the testimony of Scripture.
Ask your questions.
Examine the evidence.
Read His words.
Do not confuse honest investigation with rebellion.
Truth has nothing to fear from careful examination.
But do not mistake endless argument for the same thing as surrender.
There is a moment when the question stops being, “Can I explain every mystery?”
And becomes, “Will I trust the Savior who has been revealed?”
That is where knowledge must meet faith.
Where conviction must lead to repentance.
Where the scandal of sin meets the grace of God.
And where a life that seemed beyond repair can begin to be rewritten.
Not because the scandal never happened.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because judgment was canceled by wishful thinking.
But because Jesus Christ entered our broken world, bore our sins, rose victorious, and offers forgiveness and new life to those who come to Him.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around fear.
Not to profit from people's uncertainty about eternity.
Not to make Christians dependent on a personality or platform.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, discipleship, and the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
If this article challenged something you have always believed, don't rush past that discomfort.
Open Matthew 25.
Read Revelation 20.
Study Mark 9, Matthew 10, Romans 6, and the resurrection hope of 1 Corinthians 15.
Not to frighten them into a decision.
But to invite them into a serious, compassionate conversation about truth.
And please, don't leave this as another article you read and forget.
Do you currently believe Scripture teaches eternal conscious punishment, final destruction, or eventual restoration? Which passage has most shaped your understanding, and why?
You can disagree respectfully. You can admit uncertainty. You can even say, “I'm still studying.”
And if you have been hiding behind religious knowledge while resisting repentance, perhaps your most important comment is simply “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
You do not have to disclose private sins or painful experiences publicly to receive prayer or seek God's grace.
But honest conversations can remind struggling believers that they are not alone.
And for those who have been asking how to help this ministry continue and reach more people, there is a practical way to stand alongside us.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—an intentional expression of generosity toward Gospel outreach.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“...God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And the same verse tells us not to give grudgingly or from compulsion.
But your salvation is not for sale.
And if you cannot contribute financially, your prayers, encouragement, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share sound biblical teaching are deeply valuable.
Those items can serve as reminders of biblical truth or thoughtful gifts for someone you want to encourage, but the heart of this ministry is not merchandise.
It is Christ.
It is the Word.
It is people growing in faith and obedience.
Those free resources are part of the mission too.
You do not need to pay to begin studying, learning, or growing.
We cannot guarantee what God will do through a post, a conversation, or a ministry resource.
But we can faithfully offer what we have and leave the results in His hands.
And before you go, I want you to remember the person we imagined at the beginning.
The hospital room.
The weakening breath.
The questions no one could answer.
Maybe that scene was painfully familiar.
Maybe there is someone you miss so deeply that even reading these words brings tears.
I cannot tell you what God has not revealed about that particular person's final destiny.
And I will not manufacture certainty to make the pain disappear.
But I can tell you that the God who judges is righteous.
The Savior who died is risen.
The Gospel is still good news.
And the invitation to repent and believe is still being proclaimed to the living.
So don't let the mysteries you cannot resolve distract you from the Savior you can seek.
Don't let disagreement make you cruel.
Don't let fear become your only motivation for faith.
And don't let another day pass without considering the One who said:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” (John 11:25, KJV)
Hell is not a subject for careless speculation.
Judgment is not a weapon for humiliating people.
And grace is not permission to remain in sin.
The cross calls us to something greater.
Repentance.
Faith.
Mercy.
Truth.
A life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Because at the end of all our questions about death, destruction, punishment, and eternity, the greatest hope of the Christian is not that we have mastered every mystery.
It is that Jesus Christ has conquered the grave.
And when every argument falls silent, the question that will still matter is not whether you won the debate about judgment—but whether you heard the voice of the Savior calling you to life.
